text: The report shows every category already, but during the actual pricing review the Merchandising Manager may want to isolate or compare specific categories live. A slicer on CategoryName gives that one click of control.

Add a slicer from the Visualizations pane, drop it near the KPI cards per the layout sketch, and drag CategoryName into its field well. Set it to multi-select, since the manager might reasonably want to compare two categories side by side, not just isolate one. Because Total Sales, Order Count, and Average Order Value are all measures, every visual on the page recalculates automatically the moment the slicer selection changes -- no extra wiring needed.

Next, formatting that matches a reader glancing at this mid-meeting, not studying it. Total Sales gets currency formatting with no decimal places. Order Count gets a whole number with a thousands separator, no dollar sign. And Average Order Value gets currency with two decimal places, since a per-order average is small enough that cents can matter. Set each format once on the measure itself, so every card, chart, and table using it inherits the same format automatically.

Last step: titles. A default title like sum of TotalSalesAmount by CategoryName tells a reader what field is on the chart, not what it means. Rewriting it to something like Sales by Category states the answer instead of repeating the field name -- often the only text a time-pressed reader takes in before looking at the numbers.
With the slicer, the formatting, and the titles in place, the report is ready to leave Power BI Desktop.
Next lesson publishes it to the Power BI Service, where the Merchandising Manager can actually open it.
